newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FORECAST - Hoogovens seen recovering after lower 96.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Hoogovens seen recovering after lower 96.

text.p: Analysts expect Dutch steel and aluminium group Hoogovens to rediscover the path to higher earnings in 1997 and 1998 after a dip in 1996.

Full-year 1996 earnings due on Thursday will show a sharp drop versus 1995, but analysts expect the company to meet its own forecast that second-half net profit from normal operations will match the first-half figure of 142 million guilders.
Their forecasts of full-year net profit range from 260 to 310 million guilders with a consensus of 285 million compared with 524 million in 1995.
Hoogovens has blamed the dip in earnings last year on weak selling prices for both metals, but said that its own efforts to cut costs had partially offset this.
Analysts said aluminium prices recovered in the second half of last year, although the full benefits of this would only filter through to the bottom line this year.
With steel prices also starting to pick up this year, they predict higher profits for Hoogovens on the back of a mild economic upturn in Europe, particularly in capital spending.
Patrick Rutten at Van Lanschot sees earnings per share of 11.00 guilders in 1997 and 15.50 in 1998, up from 8.00 in 1996.
He believes the company's shares are set to outperform the rest of the Dutch market and can attain a price level of 105 guilders compared with 91.50 now.
Corne Zandbergen of Generale Bank sees EPS rising to 12.00 guilders in 1997 and 15.00 in 1998 from nine guilders last year.
He expects Hoogovens to benefit from the appreciation of sterling and the dollar which will cut import penetration from Britain and the U.S. and stimulate exports to those countries.
Analysts are also positive about the effects of Hoogovens' recently acquired 50 pct stake in Belgian steel firm UGB.
This will enable Hoogovens to process steel previously sold as semi-manufactured slabs into higher value-added steel strip and should therefore give a modest boost to earnings in time.
Continuing efforts to raise labour productivity and reduce costs are also expected to have positive long-term benefits.

Hoogovens recently struck a deal with labour unions for a phased reduction in the number of workers at its IJmuiden steel works from 10,500 to 8,500 by the year 2002, a move the company said was needed to raise productivity and stay competitive.
